passage:
Maria, eleven, was playing an online game on her mother's phone while her mother cooked. The internet kept dropping, and her little brother Zubin kept asking for a turn.
A player called StarFox99 sent a message: "You're really good! What school do you go to? Send a photo, I'll add you to our team. Don't tell your parents, they'll ruin it."
Maria's stomach went cold. Zubin was tugging her arm. The game was about to restart.
She didn't answer. She tapped the block button, then walked straight into the kitchen. "Mama, someone asked for my school and a photo and told me to keep it secret."
Her mother turned off the stove. They reported the account together that evening, and her mother set the game so strangers couldn't message her. "You did exactly right," she said.

qa.q: What did StarFox99 ask Maria for?
qa.a: What school she goes to and a photo.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when she read the message?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and alarmed; her stomach went cold.

qa.q: Which choices kept Maria safe?
qa.a: Not answering, blocking, and telling her mother right away, who reported the account and changed the settings.

qa.q: How might Maria's mother feel when Maria tells her?
qa.a: She likely feels worried but relieved and proud that Maria told her.

grounding: Shows a child refusing to share personal details and telling a trusted adult about a pressuring online contact.

On the first warm spring day in Kumasi, Kwame, eleven, and his friend Gabriel were at the river. Some older kids dared Kwame to swim across where the water was fast.
Gabriel said, "Come on, it's easy."
Kwame looked at the brown water rushing. "No. Let's swim in the shallow part."
Gabriel rolled his eyes but followed.
On the way home, Kwame told his father about the dare. His father walked back with them before dark and warned the older kids' parents.
Gabriel said, "Okay. You were right."

qa.q: Where did the older kids dare Kwame to swim?
qa.a: Across where the water was fast.

qa.q: How did Kwame feel looking at the river?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and cautious, seeing the brown water rushing.

qa.q: How did Kwame refuse without losing Gabriel?
qa.a: He offered a safer choice, swimming in the shallow part, and Gabriel followed.

qa.q: How might Kwame's father feel hearing about the dare?
qa.a: He likely feels worried but relieved Kwame said no and told him.

grounding: Shows a child refusing a risky dare and keeping a friendship, with an adult's protective step.

passage:
Monday: Farhan, eleven, was made group leader for the science model. He gave himself all the fun parts and told Ishita to just cut paper.
Wednesday: Ishita suggested using a bottle for the volcano. It worked perfectly. Farhan presented it as his idea. Ishita went quiet.
Friday: Farhan felt bad. At the class presentation he said, "The bottle idea was Ishita's. She made it work." Ishita smiled. Their teacher gave the whole group extra marks.

qa.q: What did Ishita suggest for the volcano?
qa.a: Using a bottle.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when Farhan took credit?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset, going quiet.

qa.q: What did Farhan do to make it right?
qa.a: He gave Ishita credit in front of the class.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Farhan's honesty?
qa.a: The teacher likely feels pleased, giving the group extra marks.

grounding: Tracks a child learning to share group credit fairly.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage:
Swati, you're fighting with your group about who's the leader? Let me tell you about me when I was ten, during the Onam holidays.
I, Omkar, was chosen to make the flower carpet with four others. I wanted to be the boss of everything. Nobody listened to me.
My grandmother said, "A good leader lets everyone do their best part." So I asked each one: who's good at colours, who's good at shapes? One chose colours, one shapes, one fetched flowers, I kept the pattern.
Our carpet won the colony prize. When they gave the prize, I said all our names.
So, Swati, share the work and share the credit.

qa.q: What did the group make?
qa.a: A flower carpet.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when nobody listened?
qa.a: Omkar likely felt frustrated and annoyed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Omkar's story?
qa.a: Following the grandmother's advice to let everyone do their best part and sharing roles.

qa.q: How might the group feel when Omkar says all their names?
qa.a: They likely feel proud and valued.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to share roles and credit in a group task as a child.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage:
The school's spring cleanup was due by noon, but it rained all morning. Ganga, ten, and her group had to clean the garden in half the time.
Rekha wanted to lead, but so did Ganga. They argued. Then Ganga said, "You lead. I'll carry the rubbish."
Rekha organised the team. Ganga worked hard in the mud.
When the principal praised Rekha, Rekha said, "Ganga did the heaviest work."
Ganga blushed. The principal gave the whole group a gold star for the notice board.

qa.q: When was the cleanup due?
qa.a: By noon.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when Rekha praised her?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and pleased; she blushed.

qa.q: What helped the group succeed under time pressure?
qa.a: Ganga letting Rekha lead while she did heavy work, and Rekha sharing credit.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel giving Ganga credit?
qa.a: Rekha likely feels fair and happy.

grounding: Shows children taking leader and helper roles and sharing credit fairly.
